content.intro: This lesson focuses on understanding the json data model and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding the JSON Data Model matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A JSON text contains a JSON value: an object, array, string, number, boolean, or null. Objects map string member names to values, arrays preserve order, and standard JSON syntax is stricter than a JavaScript object literal.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: JSON values. Primitive values. Structured values. Objects and arrays. Nested data structures. Valid JSON values at the document root.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as example.json and run `python -m json.tool example.json`. This validates JSON syntax and formats the file; it does not validate a JSON Schema or application business rules.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
